The little man’s body was disproportionately wide, lending his whole person a most ludicrous roundness. Naturally his feet remained entirely invisible, though now and again a suspiciously horny object projected through a tear in the bottom of the car—or, more accurately, in the crown of the hat. His hands were exceedingly huge. His hair was very grey and gathered behind into a queue. His nose was extraordinarily long, bent, and fiery; his eyes large, bright, and piercing; his cheeks and chin, though lined with years, were wide, swollen, and doubled. Yet nowhere upon his head could the slightest trace of ears, of any description whatsoever, be detected. This curious little person wore a loose sky-blue satin surtout, with close-fitting breeches of the same colour, secured at the knees by silver buckles. His waistcoat was made of some vivid yellow stuff. A white taffeta cap perched rakishly to one side of his head; and a silk handkerchief of blood-red hue completed his attire, encircling his neck and descending gracefully upon his breast in a fanciful bow of surpassing magnitude.

As I have already related, the little old gentleman had descended to within about a hundred feet of the ground when he suddenly fell into great agitation, and seemed unwilling to venture any closer to solid earth. Accordingly he lifted a canvas sack with considerable effort and scattered out a quantity of sand, whereupon his descent immediately ceased. Next, with hurried and troubled gestures, he drew a large morocco pocket-book from a side-pocket of his surtout. He balanced it mistrustfully in his hand, then regarded it with extreme surprise, plainly astonished by its heaviness. Finally he opened it and removed an enormous letter, closed with red wax and carefully secured with red tape, which he dropped directly at the feet of the burgomaster, Superbus Von Underduk. His Excellency bent to retrieve it. The aeronaut, however, remained much disconcerted and apparently had no further business requiring his presence in Rotterdam. At that instant he busied himself with preparations to leave. To rise again he had to cast off some ballast; and the half-dozen sacks which he pitched out in succession, without troubling to discharge their contents, unfortunately landed, every last one, upon the burgomaster’s back. They sent him rolling over and over at least twenty-one times before the eyes of every man in Rotterdam. It must not be imagined, however, that the mighty Underduk allowed the little old man’s insolence to go unpunished.

P.S.—Please tell me about the bows. Jennings is adamant that they are fashionable.

Lord Arthur looked so miserable and solemn as he read the letter that the Duchess burst into laughter.

“My dear Arthur,” she exclaimed, “I’ll never show you another young woman’s letter! But what should I tell her about the clock? I think it’s a wonderful invention. I’d like one myself.”

“I don’t have a very high opinion of them,” Lord Arthur said with a sorrowful smile. He kissed his mother and left the room.

Upstairs, he threw himself onto a sofa, his eyes filling with tears. He had tried his hardest to commit this murder, yet both attempts had failed through no fault of his own. He had done his best to fulfil his duty, but Destiny herself seemed to have betrayed him. The uselessness of good intentions, the futility of trying to behave nobly, weighed on him. Perhaps he should call off the marriage completely. Sybil would suffer, certainly, but suffering could never truly damage so noble a character. As for himself, what did it matter? There was always a war in which a man could die, a cause for which he could sacrifice his life. Since life offered him no pleasure, death held no fear. Let Destiny bring about his doom; he would do nothing more to assist her.

At seven-thirty he dressed and went to his club. Surbiton was there with a group of young men, and he found himself obliged to dine with them. Their shallow conversation and pointless jokes failed to interest him. As soon as the coffee arrived, he invented an appointment and escaped. On his way out, the hall porter handed him a letter from Herr Winckelkopf, inviting him to visit the following evening to inspect an explosive umbrella that detonated when opened. It was the newest invention and had just arrived from Geneva. Lord Arthur ripped the letter into small pieces. He had resolved to attempt no further experiments. He then wandered down to the Thames Embankment and sat beside the river for hours. The moon looked out through a mane of tawny clouds like the eye of a lion, while countless stars glittered across the hollow sky like gold dust scattered over a purple dome. Occasionally a barge swung into the muddy current and drifted away with the tide. The railway signals shifted from green to scarlet as trains shrieked across the bridge.

“How I wish we owned a donkey! The proper arrangement would be for all of us to ride donkeys—Jane, Miss Bates, and myself—with my caro sposo walking beside us. I must certainly speak to him of buying one. In country life I regard it as almost indispensable; for, however many occupations a woman may possess, she cannot remain perpetually indoors. And as for long walks, you know—in summer one has dust, and in winter mud.”

“You will encounter neither on the road from Highbury to Donwell. Donwell Lane is never dusty, and at present it is entirely dry. But pray ride a donkey if that suits you better. Mrs. Cole’s can be borrowed. I should like every arrangement to meet your wishes as nearly as possible.”

“Of that I am perfectly certain. I do indeed appreciate you, my dear friend. Beneath that particular dry, outspoken manner, I know yours is the kindest heart. As I tell Mr. E., you are quite a humorist. Yes, Knightley, believe me, I understand fully how attentive this whole plan is to me. You have chosen precisely what would give me pleasure.”

Mr. Knightley had an additional motive for refusing to place a table in the shade. He wanted Mr. Woodhouse, no less than Emma, to be of the company, and knew that the sight of any of them sitting outdoors for a meal would certainly make him ill. Mr. Woodhouse should not be lured into unhappiness by the plausible promise of a morning drive and an hour or two at Donwell.

The invitation was honestly meant. No concealed terrors would punish him for trusting it too readily. He agreed to come. Two years had passed since his last visit to Donwell. “On a particularly fine morning, he and Emma and Harriet might go very comfortably; he could remain seated with Mrs. Weston while the dear girls explored the gardens. Surely they could not be damp now, in the middle of the day. He would be exceedingly pleased to see the old house once more, and delighted to meet Mr. and Mrs. Elton and any of his other neighbours. He could discover no objection whatever to himself, Emma, and Harriet going on some very fine morning. Mr. Knightley had acted very properly in inviting them—most kindly and sensibly—a far cleverer arrangement than dining away from home. He did not care for dining out.”

Mr. Knightley enjoyed the good fortune of everyone’s immediate agreement. Everywhere the proposal was welcomed so warmly that all appeared, like Mrs. Elton, to regard it as a special compliment to themselves. Emma and Harriet declared that they expected immense enjoyment. Without being asked, Mr. Weston undertook to bring Frank over if he possibly could, a token of gratitude and approval that might well have been spared. Mr. Knightley was thus compelled to express his pleasure at the prospect of seeing him; and Mr. Weston promised to write without delay and employ every argument that might persuade him to come.
